paper.title: FedShard: Federated Unlearning with Efficiency Fairness and Performance Fairness
affiliations: Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou)
Hong Kong University of Science and Technology
paper.venue: AAAI-26 (Fortieth AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence)
paper.one_liner: Exact federated unlearning via a hierarchical tree of client shards that merge stage by stage, making unlearning both cheap and fair across clients.
paper.summary: When a client leaves a federated learning (FL) system, its right to be forgotten requires removing its data's influence from the global model (federated unlearning, FU). Prior FU work ignores fairness between clients. The authors define two kinds of fairness. Performance fairness: unlearning should lower accuracy only as much as the leaving client's data is unique, so remaining clients with similar data are not hurt. Efficiency fairness: the cost of unlearning a client should match its contribution and not depend on things like when it joined. Calibration-based approximate methods (FedEraser, RapidRetrain, FedRecovery) are fast but over- or under-forget, which hurts performance fairness. Exact methods are either slow (full retraining) or give very uneven costs (FATS). FedShard groups clients into shards that train in isolation and then merge stage by stage, forming a tree that ends in one global shard. Every shard's model is cached, so unlearning a client only retrains the shards on its path from leaf to root. Two adaptive algorithms keep this hierarchical training stable and fair: one merges shards with diverse update directions (A1), and one sets training rounds per shard from how varied its clients' contributions are (A2). The paper adds two fairness metrics (Mp, Me), proves exactness and an at-least-P/2 speedup, and shows FedShard avoids cascaded leaving and poisoning attacks.
paper.problem: Federated unlearning methods are judged on efficiency and effectiveness, but not on whether they are fair to clients. Approximate calibration methods cause extra accuracy loss on remaining clients, or forget too little for leaving clients (performance unfairness). Exact methods like FATS make unlearning costs depend on things like join time, so early-joined clients pay much more (efficiency unfairness). Unfair unlearning can trigger cascaded leaving of clients with similar data, and can be exploited for data poisoning attacks.
paper.core_idea: The design is 'isolated yet integrated'. Clients train in small isolated shards that are progressively merged (merging rate R) over P stages into one global shard, and every shard's model is cached. Unlearning a client retrains only the one shard per stage on its leaf-to-root path, which gives exact unlearning at a cost that depends only on the client's own path. Diversity-aware merging (A1) and variance-aware round allocation (A2) resolve the conflicts between convergence, efficiency and fairness that naive sharding creates.
paper.setting: federated (horizontal, cross-device style, client-level unlearning; supervised image classification)
contributions: FedShard, a sharded, hierarchical federated learning and unlearning framework, which the authors call the first FU method to target both performance fairness and efficiency fairness.
Two adaptive algorithms: A1, a cluster-based shard merging algorithm that promotes directional diversity, and A2, a variance-aware training-round allocation algorithm.

Formal requirements for performance fairness (P.F.) and efficiency fairness (E.F.) in FU, plus two new metrics, Mp and Me. The paper proves that minimizing them satisfies known fairness properties (envy-freeness, Pareto optimality, fairness axiom, reduction).

Theory showing exactness (equivalent to retraining) and a single-client speedup of at least P/2 over retraining from scratch. A multi-request speedup between r2- and m over one-by-one unlearning, with O(K) time for one client and O(K lg m) for m clients.

An evaluation showing that approximate FU methods cause cascaded leaving and are open to unfair-FU data poisoning attacks, and that FATS has very uneven unlearning costs. FedShard avoids all of these and unlearns 1.3-6.2x faster than retraining and up to 4.9x faster than FATS.
method_steps: Setup: K clients C = {c1..cK} and a user-chosen merging rate R (how many shards merge into one super-shard per stage). The number of stages is P (the main text writes P = ceil(K/R), but Algorithm 2 and Table 3 of the extended version use P = ceil(log_R K) with R^(P-1) < K <= R^P, so the main-text form looks like a typo). Clients are the tree's leaves, shards are its nodes and stages are its levels.

Compute each client's contribution factor alpha_c = arccos(<Delta_theta, Delta_theta_c> / (||Delta_theta||_2 ||Delta_theta_c||_2)). This is the angle between the client's local update and the global update; a smaller angle means a larger contribution. The shard-level alpha_s^p is the mean over the shard's clients.

Stage p, phase 1 (shard generation, A1): cluster the stage-(p-1) shards into 3 clusters by update-direction angle relative to the global average, using KMeans (App. D.2). Then form ceil(N_{p-1}/R) super-shards, each taking a similar number of shards from every cluster (children chosen to minimize Me), so each new shard mixes average, large-positive and large-negative directions.

Stage p, phase 2 (shard initialization and round allocation, A2): initialize each new shard's model theta_s^{p,0} from its children. Pick rounds T_s^p in a range [T0*, T1*] taken from a preliminary run (min and max rounds to converge in early stages, e.g. [4,7]), using Eq. 2: (T_s^p - T0*)/(T1* - T0*) = [(sigma^2(alpha_s^p) - sigma^2_min)/(sigma^2_max - sigma^2_min)]^(-1). Homogeneous shards (low contribution variance) get more rounds and heterogeneous ones get fewer.

Stage p, phase 3 (parallel federated training): each shard runs federated training (FedAvg-style aggregation with weights w_s^p) over its own clients only, for T_s^p rounds, in parallel with the other shards.

Stage p, phase 4 (state caching): the server stores each shard's membership, T_s^p, initial model theta_s^{p,0}, trained model theta_s^p, alpha_s^p and w_s^p in FLCache. Repeat until stage P has one shard with all clients. Its model theta_1^P is the global model. Space is O(K), the same order as FedAvg.

Unlearning (Algorithm 1): when client c_l asks to leave, find the affected shards (the one shard per stage that contains c_l, i.e. its leaf-to-root path). For p = 1..P, retrain each affected shard from its initial state with the remaining clients for T_s^p rounds. Unaffected shards reuse their cached models. Update FLCache with the retrained shards. Return theta_u* = theta_1^P.

Multiple simultaneous requests: retrain the union of all affected paths in one pass. Shared ancestors are retrained once, and after stage p' every shard contains a leaving client. This gives an extra speedup between r2- and m over unlearning the clients one by one.

key_definitions.name: Performance fairness (P.F.)
key_definitions.plain: Unlearning should cause a fair accuracy drop across clients. A leaving client with unique data should be forgotten fully, which may cause a large drop on its data. Remaining clients whose data resembles the leaver's should not suffer an excessive drop, since their data is still in the system. This protects both the leaver's RTBF and the remaining clients' right to good model performance.

key_definitions.name: Efficiency fairness (E.F.)
key_definitions.plain: Every client should face a fair unlearning cost when it leaves. The cost should depend only on its own contribution or impact, not on factors like join time or shard placement. Unequal leaving costs discourage clients from participating.

key_definitions.name: Contribution factor alpha_c
key_definitions.plain: The angle between a client's local update and the global update, used as the client's impact on the global model. A smaller angle means a larger contribution. Loss similarity, Shapley value or information entropy could replace it (App. C).
key_definitions.formal: alpha_c = arccos( <Delta_theta, Delta_theta_c> / (||Delta_theta||_2 * ||Delta_theta_c||_2) ); alpha_s^p = mean of alpha_c over clients in shard S_s^p

key_definitions.name: Data distance Dis
key_definitions.plain: How different two clients' data are, judged by their contribution angles.

key_definitions.name: Performance fairness metric Mp
key_definitions.plain: For each client, it compares the accuracy drop on its data caused by unlearning with how unique its data is (distance to the nearest remaining client). f_plus is lowest when the two normalized values match: unique leavers should get a big drop, and clients with lookalike remaining data should get a small one.
key_definitions.formal: Mp = (1/|C|) * sum_{c in C} f_plus( Delta_Y(D_c), min_{c_r in C_R} Dis(c, c_r) ); f_plus(x,y) = (x~ + y~) * (1/x~ + 1/y~), convex, minimized at x~ = y~; x~ = eps + (x - x_min)/(x_max - x_min) in (0,1]

key_definitions.name: Efficiency fairness metric Me
key_definitions.plain: The contribution-weighted variance of unlearning costs (computing time) across clients. If two clients contribute about the same but cost very different amounts to unlearn, Me is large.
key_definitions.formal: Me = (1/|C|) * sum_{c in C} (Z_avg - Z_c)^2 / |alpha_c|, where Z_c = unlearning cost (time) of client c and Z_avg = mean cost

key_definitions.name: Merging rate R and stages P
key_definitions.plain: R is how many shards merge into one super-shard at the next stage. P is the number of stages, or tree levels.
key_definitions.formal: Main text: P = ceil(K/R). Extended version, Alg. 2 / Table 3: P = ceil(log_R K), with R^(P-1) < K <= R^P.

key_definitions.name: Variance-aware round allocation (Eq. 2)
key_definitions.plain: Sets a shard's training rounds inversely to how varied its clients' contributions are. This avoids overfitting divergent shards and avoids under-training.

key_definitions.name: Cascaded leaving
key_definitions.plain: Unfair unlearning causes a large accuracy drop for remaining clients with data similar to the leaver's, which pushes them to leave too. This chain reaction threatens the FL system's sustainability. In the App. G.5 simulation, a remaining client leaves when Delta_Y > Y* - Z.
key_definitions.formal: Remaining-client payoff: stay W_r^k = -Delta_Y - Z + lambda_r, leave W_r^l = -Y* + lambda_r (extended version App. G.5)

key_definitions.name: Unfair-FU data poisoning attack (uf-DPA)
key_definitions.plain: Malicious clients join, train on data that resembles a target group's, and then request unlearning. A performance-unfair FU method over-unlearns, which degrades the targeted remaining clients.
key_definitions.formal: DPA precision = (# successfully poisoned clients) / (total # clients)

theory.name: Proposition 1 (exactness) + induction
theory.statement_plain: A training run whose dataset excludes D_l and whose initial model is not affected by D_l can be reused as-is when unlearning D_l, and this equals retraining from scratch on D0 \ D_l. By induction over stages, retraining only the shard that contains the leaver at each stage (with all other shards cached) is as effective as retraining from scratch.
theory.assumptions: The cached states of unaffected shards were never influenced by the leaver's data. The paper calls this assumption standard in the exact-unlearning literature (SISA, FATS, Exact-Fun). Whether the shard structure and round choices, which were computed while the leaver was present, also need recomputing is not discussed.
theory.significance: Makes FedShard exact unlearning, so it is performance-fair by construction (no over- or under-forgetting).

theory.name: Proposition 2 (single-client speedup, constant rounds T0)
theory.statement_plain: FedShard unlearning is r1 times faster than vanilla retraining (FedAvg from scratch).
theory.assumptions: Every shard trains for the same T0 rounds. R is a positive integer.
theory.significance: r1 = ((R-1)/R) * (K/(K-1)) * P >= P/2 (usually about P): the speedup grows with the number of stages.

theory.name: Proposition 3 (general case, variable rounds)
theory.statement_plain: With per-shard rounds between Tmin and Tmax, the speedup r1_hat satisfies r1*T0/Tmax <= r1_hat <= r1*T0/Tmin.
theory.assumptions: Rounds are set by A2 within [Tmin, Tmax].
theory.significance: Keeping the round range narrow (the goal of A2) keeps unlearning both efficient and fair. This is the theoretical case for A2.

theory.name: Proposition 4 (multiple simultaneous requests)
theory.statement_plain: Unlearning m clients together is between r2- and r2+ times faster than unlearning them one by one, with r2+ = m and r2- = (R/(R-1)) * ((K-1)/K) * m/(P - p') >= 1. Here p' is the stage after which every shard contains a leaving client.
theory.assumptions: The m clients leave at the same time.
theory.significance: Batching unlearning requests is never worse and can be up to m times better.

theory.name: Corollary 1 (time complexity)
theory.statement_plain: FedShard unlearning takes O(K) time for one client and O(K lg m) time for m clients. Space is O(K), the same as FedAvg, per extended version App. E/D.1.
theory.significance: Gives a sublinear-in-m cost for batched deletions.

theory.name: Fairness properties of Mp and Me (Sec. 5.3; App. F, Props. 5-16 in extended version)
theory.statement_plain: FU algorithms that minimize Mp satisfy envy-freeness (FP.1), Pareto optimality (FP.2) and the fairness axiom (FP.3). Those that minimize Me satisfy the fairness axiom (FP.3) and reduction (FP.4). The appendix also lists continuity, homogeneity, non-saturation, partition and starvation for Mp, and reduction-to-equality, continuity, non-homogeneity, saturation and partition for Me.
theory.assumptions: Absolute Mp and Me values are meaningful only when comparing FU methods under identical settings. The two metrics are designed to be orthogonal.
theory.significance: Grounds the new unlearning-fairness metrics in axiomatic fairness theory from economics and networking (Lan et al. 2010; Feldman and Kirman 1974; Li and Xue 2013).

theory.name: Convergence (not proven)
theory.statement_plain: The paper gives no formal convergence bound for sharded hierarchical training. Convergence is argued informally (diverse merging, bounded rounds) and shown empirically (ablation, Fig. 5).
theory.significance: There is also no formal fairness bound: P.F. follows from exactness, and E.F. is argued via the bounded round range (Prop. 3) and shown empirically.

paper.complexity: Learning: P stages of parallel per-shard FL. The server stores per-shard, per-stage models and metadata in FLCache, which is O(K) space (same order as FedAvg; extended version). Unlearning one client retrains one shard per stage along its leaf-to-root path. That is O(K) time and at least P/2 times (usually about P times) faster than FedAvg retraining with equal rounds; with variable rounds the speedup is scaled by T0/Tmax to T0/Tmin. m simultaneous requests take O(K lg m) time, between r2- and m times faster than sequential. Communication cost is not analyzed separately; retraining still needs the remaining clients in affected shards to take part.

datasets: EMNIST, SVHN, Purchase, Adult (appendix of arXiv extended version only; not in the AAAI PDF)
models: 2-layer CNN as in FedAvg (McMahan et al. 2017)
baselines: FA: vanilla retraining from scratch via FedAvg (exact)
RR: RapidRetrain (Liu et al. 2022, Hessian-based calibration/approximate)
FR: FedRecovery (Zhang et al. 2023b, DP-based approximate)
headline_results: Abstract/intro: FedShard unlearns 1.3-6.2x faster than retraining from scratch and up to 4.9x faster than state-of-the-art exact unlearning (FATS). The exact settings behind 6.2x and 4.9x are in appendix G.2/G.3 and are not shown in the main-text tables.

Table 1 (K=512, rho=0.1): FS unlearning time on MNIST/FMNIST/CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100 = 2485.1/2508.3/3361.1/6859.2 s vs FA 9244.6/9984.4/13459.3/29660.2 s (about 3.7-4.3x faster) and FT 6832.1/6163.7/8403.9/16822.5 s (about 2.5-2.8x faster). FR is far faster (10-18 s) but approximate.
Performance fairness Mp (Table 1): FS 6.08/5.95/6.08/5.94, close to FA (5.68-6.35) and FT (6.46-7.13); approximate methods are worse: FE 9.4-11.7, RR 9.2-10.9, FR 14.0-22.1.
Ablation (CIFAR-10, K=32, R=2, rho=0.1, 30 epochs): FedAvg 62.92%; naive sharding without A1/A2 collapses after each merge; with A1 only 56.3%; with A1+A2 64.14%, beating FedAvg.
Table 2 (CIFAR-10): MIA F1 non-unlearned 91.37; FA 34.18, FS 35.04, FT 36.07 vs over-forgetting FE 30.14, RR 28.65, FR 25.07. DPA precision: FA/FT/FS 0%, FE 20.83%, RR 22.91%, FR 28.50%.
Fig. 7: RR and FE have high Mp and cause cascaded leaving, more so as the data becomes more IID (higher rho). FS, FA and FT cause no cascaded leaving.
Fig. 6 (CIFAR-10, 256 clients): FT's per-client unlearning costs vary widely, while FS's are low and tightly concentrated.
Extended version: about 27% faster than retraining at K=32 and 3.7x at K=512. Speedup grows with the number of clients.

limitations: Client-level unlearning only (a whole client leaves). Sample-level deletion inside a client is not handled.
No formal convergence guarantee for hierarchical sharded training. Stability relies on the empirical A1/A2 heuristics, and naive sharding collapses.
[T0*, T1*] comes from a preliminary run (extra tuning cost). A1 uses a fixed 3-cluster KMeans.

Possible exactness subtlety (noticed, not discussed): the shard structure (A1 clustering on alpha), the round counts (A2 variance) and the normalization in Eq. 2 were computed while the leaving client was present. If they are not recomputed, the unlearned model may not match running FedShard from scratch without that client.

Notation inconsistencies: P = ceil(K/R) in the main text vs ceil(log_R K) in the extended version's algorithm. Table 1's caption says K=512 while Sec. 6.2 says 256 clients. The 6.2x and 4.9x headline numbers are not visible in the main-text tables.
FedShard is 'one of the fastest' only among exact methods. FedRecovery unlearns in about 10-18 s vs FedShard's 2,500-6,900 s.

Mp and Me are relative, setting-dependent scores. Me divides by |alpha_c|, so clients with a very small angle (the largest contributors) weight cost deviations very heavily, and alpha near 0 blows up. Both metrics depend on the chosen contribution factor.
Experiments use small models (2-layer CNN) and up to 512 clients; scaling beyond 1,000 clients is left to future work.
Every unlearning request must retrain at least the final global stage, and remaining clients in affected shards must come back online to retrain.
future_work: Scaling to more than 1,000 clients (stated in extended version).
Other contribution factors (loss similarity, Shapley value, information entropy), discussed in App. C.
Suggested by this extraction: dynamic client arrival, and sample-level unlearning within the hierarchy.
paper.relevance_to_efficient_unlearning: FedShard shows how to carry SISA-style exact unlearning (sharding plus cached checkpoints) into federated learning. Instead of an ensemble of isolated shard models, it uses a tree of progressively merged shards, so retraining is limited to one leaf-to-root path of P nodes. Its speedup analysis (r1 >= P/2, bounds under variable rounds, batch speedup between r2- and m, O(K lg m) for m deletions) is a reusable template for analyzing hierarchical or divide-and-conquer unlearning. Mp and Me add a new evaluation axis: who pays for unlearning and who gets hurt by it. Me in particular could be applied to SISA, where unlearning cost depends on shard and slice position. Pitfalls to note: naive merging of shard models can collapse accuracy, and structure choices made from data that is later forgotten may break strict exactness.
open_questions: Make FedShard strictly exact under deletion of structure-defining clients. Either make A1/A2 decisions independent of the leaver's updates or recompute them cheaply, and prove equivalence to running FedShard from scratch without that client.
Prove a convergence bound for hierarchical shard-merging FL that depends on R, P, rounds T_s^p and directional diversity (e.g. under bounded heterogeneity).
Design an Me-style efficiency-fairness metric and a cost-equalizing shard/slice assignment for centralized SISA, where unlearning cost depends on slice position.
Combine FedShard's client-level tree with SISA-style slicing inside each client for sample-level federated unlearning, and analyze the combined speedup.
Extend the hierarchy to dynamic joining or continual settings (clients arrive over time), avoiding the join-time cost unfairness seen in FATS.
Apply Mp/Me-type fairness auditing to federated clustering unlearning (e.g. MUFC) or to group-fairness-aware unlearning (FairSISA).

nodes.label: Federated Learning
nodes.description: Collaborative training where clients keep their data locally and a server aggregates model updates into a shared global model.

nodes.label: Federated Unlearning
nodes.description: Removing the contribution of particular clients or data from a model trained by federated learning, without central access to raw data.

nodes.label: Machine Unlearning
nodes.description: Removing the influence of specific training data from a trained model so it behaves as if that data had never been used.

nodes.label: Exact Unlearning
nodes.description: Unlearning whose output is identical (or identically distributed) to retraining from scratch without the deleted data.

nodes.label: Approximate Unlearning
nodes.description: Unlearning that only approximates the retrained model, usually by adjusting parameters, trading guarantees for speed.

nodes.label: Right to be Forgotten
nodes.description: Legal right (e.g. GDPR, CCPA) for individuals to have their personal data, and its effects, erased.

nodes.label: Fairness
nodes.description: The principle that a system's outcomes or costs should be distributed equitably across individuals or groups.

nodes.label: Client Fairness
nodes.description: Fairness across participating clients in federated learning, e.g. in performance, rewards or costs.

nodes.label: Efficiency Fairness
nodes.description: In unlearning, the requirement that the cost of removing a client is fair, i.e. depends on that client's own contribution rather than incidental factors like join time.

nodes.label: Performance Fairness
nodes.description: In unlearning, the requirement that performance degradation from unlearning is distributed fairly. Leavers' data is fully forgotten, while remaining clients with similar data are not excessively hurt.

nodes.label: Batch Unlearning
nodes.description: Processing several deletion requests together so shared retraining work is done once.

nodes.label: Clustered Federated Learning
nodes.description: FL variant that groups clients into clusters and trains a separate model per cluster to handle heterogeneity.

nodes.label: K-means Clustering
nodes.description: Partitioning points into k groups by minimizing within-cluster squared distances to centroids.

nodes.label: Differential Privacy
nodes.description: A formal privacy guarantee that limits how much any single record can change an algorithm's output distribution.

nodes.label: FedShard
nodes.description: Exact federated unlearning framework that trains clients in a hierarchy of isolated shards merged stage by stage, and caches shard models so unlearning retrains only the leaver's leaf-to-root path.

nodes.label: Hierarchical Shard Tree
nodes.description: Organizing training participants into shards that are progressively merged (R at a time) across stages, forming a tree whose root is a single global shard.

nodes.label: Cluster-based Shard Merging (A1)
nodes.description: Shard merging rule that clusters shards by update direction (KMeans, 3 clusters) and builds each super-shard from different clusters so it is directionally diverse and representative.

nodes.label: Variance-aware Round Allocation (A2)
nodes.description: Assigns per-shard training rounds within an empirically set range [T0*, T1*], inversely to the variance of client contributions in the shard.

nodes.label: Data Sharding
nodes.description: Splitting training data (or data owners) into disjoint shards trained in isolation, so a deletion only affects one shard.

nodes.label: Checkpointing / Caching Intermediate Models
nodes.description: Storing intermediate model states during training so later retraining can resume from a state unaffected by deleted data.

nodes.label: SISA
nodes.description: Sharded, Isolated, Sliced, Aggregated training: exact unlearning by training isolated models on disjoint data shards (with slice checkpoints) and retraining only the affected shard.

nodes.label: FedAvg
nodes.description: Federated Averaging: clients run local SGD and the server averages their models weighted by data size.

nodes.label: Retrain from Scratch
nodes.description: The gold-standard exact unlearning baseline that retrains the model on the remaining data only.

nodes.label: Calibration-based Federated Unlearning
nodes.description: Approximate FU that removes a client by adjusting (calibrating) the global model's parameters, e.g. with cached updates, Hessian corrections or gradient ascent, instead of retraining.

nodes.label: FedEraser
nodes.description: Approximate federated unlearning that reconstructs the unlearned model by calibrating cached historical client updates with a few rounds of remaining-client training.

nodes.label: RapidRetrain
nodes.description: Federated unlearning method that speeds up retraining using a diagonal-Hessian (Fisher) approximation for quick parameter correction.

nodes.label: FedRecovery
nodes.description: Differentially private approximate federated unlearning that subtracts a weighted sum of the leaver's gradient residuals and adds noise.

nodes.label: FATS
nodes.description: Communication-efficient, provable exact federated unlearning (Tao et al. 2024) that uses client and sample sampling with cached states so unlearning can skip rounds in which the leaver did not take part.

nodes.label: Exact-Fun
nodes.description: Exact and efficient federated unlearning approach (Xiong et al. 2023) that reuses cached information to reduce retraining cost.

nodes.label: ShardingEraser
nodes.description: Federated unlearning method that applies sharding to accelerate the approximate FedEraser procedure.

nodes.label: Gradient Ascent Unlearning
nodes.description: Approximate unlearning by maximizing the loss on data to be forgotten.

nodes.label: Unfairness
nodes.description: Inequitable distribution of a system's outcomes or costs across individuals or groups.

nodes.label: Cascaded Leaving
nodes.description: Chain reaction where one client's departure (via unfair unlearning) degrades similar remaining clients, prompting them to leave too.

nodes.label: Data Poisoning Attack
nodes.description: Adversaries inject or manipulate training data or updates to degrade or control a model's behavior.

nodes.label: Unfair-FU Poisoning Attack (uf-DPA)
nodes.description: Attack that abuses unlearning requests. Malicious participants with data resembling a target group's join and then ask to be forgotten, so an over-unlearning method degrades the targets.

nodes.label: Membership Inference Attack
nodes.description: Attack that infers whether a specific record was in a model's training set. In unlearning it is used to test whether deleted data is still detectable.

nodes.label: Unlearning Cost
nodes.description: Computation, time or communication required to remove data's influence from a trained model.

nodes.label: Utility Degradation
nodes.description: Loss of model accuracy or usefulness on retained data caused by unlearning.

nodes.label: Data Heterogeneity (Non-IID)
nodes.description: Clients' local data distributions differ, which slows or destabilizes federated training.

nodes.label: Over-/Insufficient Unlearning
nodes.description: Approximate unlearning removes more than the target data's influence (hurting similar retained data) or too little (leaving residual influence).

nodes.label: Convergence-Efficiency-Fairness Dilemma
nodes.description: In sharded training, choices that equalize or cut unlearning cost (merging similar shards, many isolated rounds) can hurt convergence and global accuracy, and vice versa.

nodes.label: Merge-induced Model Collapse
nodes.description: Sharp accuracy drop and failure to re-converge when separately trained shard models are naively merged.

nodes.label: Unlearning Guarantee (Exactness)
nodes.description: Formal statement that an unlearning procedure's output is equivalent to retraining without the deleted data.

nodes.label: FedShard Single-client Speedup Bound
nodes.description: FedShard's single-client speedup over retraining: r1 = ((R-1)/R)(K/(K-1))P >= P/2 for constant rounds, and r1*T0/Tmax <= r1_hat <= r1*T0/Tmin with variable rounds.

nodes.label: FedShard Multi-request Speedup Bound
nodes.description: Speedup of batched over sequential unlearning of m clients, between r2- = (R/(R-1))((K-1)/K)(m/(P-p')) >= 1 and r2+ = m.

nodes.label: Deletion Efficiency
nodes.description: Property that the cost of processing a deletion is much lower than full retraining, e.g. sublinear in dataset or participant count.

nodes.label: Envy-freeness
nodes.description: Fair-division property: no agent prefers another agent's allocation to its own.

nodes.label: Pareto Optimality
nodes.description: An allocation where no agent can be made better off without making another worse off.

nodes.label: Axiomatic Fairness Measure Properties
nodes.description: Axioms such as continuity, homogeneity, saturation, partition and starvation that a fairness measure should satisfy (Lan et al. 2010).

nodes.label: Reduction (to Equality) Property
nodes.description: Fairness-measure property that the measure reduces to perfect fairness when all agents receive equal allocations or costs.

nodes.label: Mp (Performance Fairness Metric)
nodes.description: Average convex mismatch f_plus between each client's normalized accuracy drop from unlearning and its normalized data uniqueness (distance to the nearest remaining client). Lower is fairer.

nodes.label: Me (Efficiency Fairness Metric)
nodes.description: Contribution-weighted variance of per-client unlearning costs: mean of (Z_avg - Z_c)^2 / |alpha_c|. Lower is fairer.

nodes.label: Contribution Factor (Update Angle)
nodes.description: Measure of a participant's impact on the global model. FedShard uses the angle arccos(cos-sim) between a local update and the global update, where smaller means a bigger contribution.

nodes.label: Unlearning Time
nodes.description: Wall-clock or compute time needed to complete an unlearning request.

nodes.label: Speedup

cross_paper.note: FedShard carries SISA's sharded, isolated retraining into FL as a hierarchical, merging tree of client shards. It cites SISA for Proposition 1 (cached unaffected states give exact unlearning) and rejects plain SISA in FL because SISA needs central data access.

Both combine sharded exact unlearning with fairness. FairSISA targets group fairness (e.g. equalized odds) of SISA ensembles, while FedShard targets client-level performance and cost fairness of unlearning itself.
Both do exact, efficient client-level unlearning in federated settings (MUFC for federated clustering, FedShard for supervised FL). FedShard's Mp/Me fairness metrics could audit MUFC.

Ginart et al.'s divide-and-conquer DC-k-means uses a tree of sub-problems where a deletion only reruns the affected leaf-to-root path. FedShard's hierarchical shard tree applies the same idea to federated deep learning.
Both study client-level fairness in federated settings. FedShard contrasts itself with clustered FL, which lacks a unified global model for exact unlearning.
MeCo's federated continual learning on edge systems faces clients joining and leaving. FedShard's sharded caching and fairness metrics show how departures could be unlearned fairly there.
